doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Teaching the non-musical side, Hinton's openness and jazz characters
summary: Few minority students at the conference, Hinton's open-door attitude, encouragement from elders, and the loss of strong characters like Joe Williams, Dizzy, Moody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: How important is it that students learn about the parts of being a musician that aren’t just the music. Punctuality and personality. As a matter of fact I think you summed it up “hanging on the bandstand” I think was your —

Well, you know I really want — if the players really want it, it’s here for them. There is a lot of talk about, I mean just here at the conference, there aren’t a whole lot of minority kids here. So that’s kind of disconcerting to a point. But like Milton Hinton, he said if a young woman wanted to play, he could care less if you are a girl, blue, green, purple. If you wanted to play and you wanted to learn something from him, it’s yours. Whatever you’ve got is yours. And I feel the same way. The music knows no colors, has no boundaries. And I think some people dwell on that kind of stuff and you can’t do that. I mean it does a disservice to everybody, particularly the music. But I want to show, when I see young people, if they’re willing to listen I’m willing to work with them. Because people helped me, I mean all I needed was maybe a pat on the back and that was huge. That gave me — from someone I had a lot of respect for, or I didn’t expect. Because mostly they didn’t have to say anything. And if they didn’t really care about you they didn’t say anything. Or, “that’s not really that good, you play better than that, don’t do that again.” They don’t have to do that.
Right. If they had kept quiet you’d have just kept doing it.

And then eventually you fade away. So in a sense these educational things are good. We are giving a craft that students are learning a craft, but that doesn’t mean that they’re going to be great musicians. The music that — I mean you had a film of a character. Joe Williams was a character. I mean he was an entity. I mean he was something special. And

I think Dizzy, James Moody, Sonny Stitt, Wes Montgomery. I mean these are people that just were characters. But they had a lot of excellence. You don’t have to just be a fool. You know nobody wants to be around that. And so in a sense we are not allowing the characters to come through all this, because there’s a lot of cookie cutters now. There’s a lot of — and it’s really hard for the character to come through now, because there’s probably a little more suppressed stuff for someone who wants to go this way and the masses are going over here. Because to be different, you have to be very strong.
